title: Topic 3 Changing ecosystems - Hodder practice questions

questions.question_text: Figure 3.23 shows a food web for the sea around Antarctica. Identify the main source of energy for this ecosystem.

points: Solar energy / the Sun [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award 1 mark for Solar energy or the Sun.

questions.question_text: Identify the organism that feeds on phytoplankton.

points: Zooplankton (or krill) [1]

questions.question_text: State the organism that feeds on birds.

points: Seals (or Leopard seals) [1]

questions.question_text: State the top carnivore in the Antarctic marine ecosystem.

points: Toothed whales (or Killer whales / Orcas) [1]

questions.question_text: Explain why Antarctica's ecosystems are largely marine-based rather than land-based.

points: The land is covered in ice and too cold for almost all plant growth [1]
There is negligible terrestrial vegetation/soil, so the land cannot support herbivorous animals [1]
It is dark for much of the winter, severely limiting land photosynthesis [1]
The surrounding Southern Ocean is nutrient-rich due to upwelling currents, supporting enormous blooms of phytoplankton and krill [1]
Terrestrial land is used mainly as breeding ground (penguins, seals) free from land predators [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award up to 3 marks for explaining why land cannot support life vs why the ocean is rich in nutrients.

questions.question_text: View Figure 3.16 on page 80 which shows an area of tropical rainforest. Identify how this area of rainforest is being used.

points: Agriculture / commercial farming / cattle ranching / plantation (oil palm / soya) [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award 1 mark for agriculture, farming, cattle ranching, or plantation.

questions.question_text: Compare the characteristics of the vegetation in the rainforest with that of the cleared area.

points: The rainforest has high biodiversity with dense, stratified layers of trees (canopy, emergent, undercanopy) [1]
The cleared area has very low biodiversity, consisting of monoculture / grass / bare soil / single crop species [1]
Trees are tall and evergreen in rainforest, whereas the cleared area has short grasses or low crops [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award up to 2 marks for comparative statements between rainforest vegetation and cleared area.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why tropical rainforests are being destroyed by human activities.

points: Reason 1: Commercial agriculture and cattle ranching (e.g. Amazon basin) to produce beef and soya for export [1], requiring clear-felling of large tracts of forest [1]
Reason 2: Logging for valuable tropical hardwoods (e.g. mahogany, teak) or pulp [1], opening up roads into pristine forest [1]

Other valid reasons: Mineral extraction / mining (e.g. Carajás iron ore); Hydroelectric power (HEP) dam construction flooding valleys; Infrastructure / road building (e.g. Trans-Amazonian Highway) [1-2 marks each]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award 2 marks for each well-explained reason (1 mark identification, 1 mark elaboration). Maximum 4 marks.

questions.question_text: Explain the consequences of the deforestation of tropical rainforests.

points: Loss of biodiversity and habitat: extinction of unique plant and animal species and loss of potential medicinal plants [1]
Soil erosion and nutrient leaching: removal of tree canopy exposes topsoil to intense tropical rainfall, washing away nutrients and silting rivers [1]
Contribution to climate change / enhanced greenhouse effect: burning trees releases stored CO₂, and loss of trees reduces carbon sink capacity [1]
Disruption of local water cycle: less transpiration leads to reduced rainfall, drier local climate, and increased flash flooding risk [1]
Impact on indigenous tribes: displacement and loss of traditional livelihoods and culture [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award up to 4 marks for explaining ecological, climatic, or social consequences of deforestation.
